summary: Round 2 of M4.20. R1 is genuinely closed -- I reproduced both mutations against the staged tests and each dies. R7 is closed. The four minors recorded on other rows are recorded, and three of the four accurately. But R2 IS NOT FIXED AT ALL: the 'WHAT IT DOES NOT DO YET' paragraph in CommitProtocolSimulation.java is byte-for-byte the round-1 text -- both false claims still stand -- and no baselines/review.txt entry argues it. Nothing was rewritten; there is no new concurrency comment to overclaim in either direction. Two of the rows that received recorded minors misstate what was found (M4.22 overstates, M4.10 inverts the consequence), and the withZone fix leaves the copy's OWN withZone unconstrained -- the same contract defect one level down, in code this commit adds.

findings.summary: CARRIED FORWARD UNCHANGED, not fixed and not argued. The paragraph reads, verbatim from round 1: 'pods here take turns rather than running concurrently, so this reaches interleavings of FAILOVER but not of two writers racing one slot in real time. `LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest` covers that at the unit level; carrying it into the simulation is M4.13's.' I verified the staged bytes directly (git show :sequencer/.../CommitProtocolSimulation.java) and the worktree equals the index (git diff --stat empty), so there is no unstaged revision either, and baselines/review.txt contains only the M0.31-R3-1 entry -- so the finding was neither fixed nor argued. Every claim of the round-1 finding re-verified against the tree today: LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest.java has exactly ONE @Test, aLosingConcurrentAcquireCannotWipeTheWinnersBeliefOnTheSameInstance (line 37), which races the LEASE key inside one LeaseManager; the CHAIN-slot race lives in CommitLogSealWriteTest.sealingRedrivesPastADeltaTheOldLeaderWonRatherThanSurrenderingTheCluster (line 81, with its oldLeaderCommits helper at line 54) and in LocalSequencerTest lines 238 and 267 via StealFirstPutStore; M4.13's row (backlog line 273) owns the 1,000-seed sweep, delayed writes, reordered completions, partitioned leaders as an injectable fault and the withheld-write ambiguity and says nothing about concurrent pods; and FaultInjectingStore.java:144-153 still instructs the OPPOSITE in as many words -- 'THIS IS A NOTE TO M4.20 ... interleave them LOGICALLY, one call at a time from one thread, rather than one virtual thread per pod. Concurrency there would not corrupt the store, it would corrupt REPRODUCIBILITY'. The comment also still frames turn-taking as a limitation ('WHAT IT DOES NOT DO YET') when the store in the same package requires it.
findings.failure_scenario: Unchanged from round 1 and now one round more likely to land. A reader auditing M4's completion condition follows this javadoc to LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest, finds a green test about the LEASE key, and concludes the one-slot race is covered at the unit level -- it is not covered there, it is covered in CommitLogSealWriteTest and LocalSequencerTest, so an audit that removed either of those would report the coverage intact. Meanwhile M4.13 is picked up from its own row, which never mentions concurrency, so nobody carries the real-time slot race anywhere; and whoever DOES act on the sentence gives each pod a virtual thread, which FaultInjectingStore's unsynchronised ArrayList/TreeMap and per-call stream order turn into a run that no longer replays from its seed -- destroying the named-regression property every assertion in CommitProtocolSimulationTest rests on.

findings.summary: The R1 fix introduces a second withZone -- the re-zoned copy's own -- and nothing constrains it. MEASURED on the staged tree: replacing `return outer.withZone(other);` with `return this;` leaves all four SimulatedClockTest tests green (BUILD SUCCESSFUL), because no test ever re-zones the copy. That is precisely the defect this commit exists to fix (an object that reports the old zone while agreeing it was re-zoned), reproduced one level down in code the commit adds, under a javadoc at lines 46-52 that asserts Clock-contract conformance for withZone generally. For contrast, the two mutations the fix DOES kill, both reproduced here: `withZone` returning `this` fails withZoneReturnsACLOCKCarryingTheGivenZoneAndTheSAMETime only, and the JDK's snapshotting shape (`if (zone.equals(getZone())) return this; return Clock.fixed(instant(), zone);`) fails aReZonedCopySTILLMovesWhenTheOriginalAdvances only -- so R1 is closed by the Australia/Sydney change, and this is the arm the change did not reach.
findings.failure_scenario: A later consumer -- a LeaseManager fixture, or M4.13 driving pods that each want a zoned view -- calls clock.withZone(SYDNEY).withZone(TOKYO) and gets back a clock reporting Australia/Sydney. It advances with the original, so every delegation test still passes and every time-based assertion still holds; only a formatted timestamp in a log line or an assertion on getZone() is wrong, which is the silent-wrong-zone failure the class javadoc says would 'have been found the hard way'. One assertion on zoned.withZone(TOKYO).getZone() closes it.

findings.summary: The M4.22 row records R5 with a stronger claim than R5 measured, and the stronger claim is false. It says '`Result` reports no productivity measure at all -- so a run that spent 90% of its rounds leaderless is indistinguishable from a healthy one in everything it returns'. Result carries `commits` and `takeovers`, and those DO separate the two cases loudly: round 1 measured 208 commits at ROUGH against 2,133 for the same seeds CLEAN, and the staged test's own comment records the clean run's WORST seed at 52 commits against a ROUGH range of 0..21 -- a factor of ten, visible in the first field of the record. What R5 actually found is narrower and still true: Result reports no measure of how many ROUNDS were productive (300 of 3,600 had a leader, 3,223 ended with tryStart empty), so a change that halves the rounds reaching commit() can hide under floors that only look at totals.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.22 is picked up and its author reads 'no productivity measure at all', looks at Result, sees commits and takeovers, and concludes the row is describing something that is not there -- the row loses its credibility on the sentence that is meant to hand over the work, exactly as the M4.20 row itself records happening once already when a defect note pointed at M4.16. Or worse, the author 'fixes' it by adding a commits accessor that already exists and closes the row, leaving the rounds-productive gap open with a row marked done over it.

findings.summary: The M4.10 row records R8's mechanism correctly and then inverts its consequence. The new clause ends '-- the harness therefore cannot currently express the very duplicate this row exists to suppress', but the mechanism it just described produces the opposite hazard: a flushSeq REPEATED after a failure is a repeat by the same pod, so it is exactly the shape M4.10's dedup would key on, and R8's scenario was that M4.10 would then drop a REAL second commit (pod1 commits seg/40 at flushSeq 7 under an ambiguousPut that lands, stands down without incrementing, re-acquires and commits a DIFFERENT segment seg/45 at flushSeq 7). That consequence -- the harness generating traffic that violates the key's stated uniqueness -- is the part a reader of M4.10 needs and it is the part the row drops. Two details of the mechanism are also lost: there are TWO independent global counters, `commits` for the leader path and `zombieWrites` for the zombie path, and since a zombie's pod string can be re-picked as the next leader (random.nextInt(pods) over three names), the two counters can collide on the SAME podId; and R8's stated fix, a Map<String, Long> incremented on every ATTEMPT, is not carried over.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10 is implemented from this row. Its author reads 'the harness cannot express the duplicate', concludes the simulation needs a new retry path to produce one, adds it, and does not fix the counter -- so the first sweep after the dedup lands drops legitimate commits wherever a leader stood down and re-acquired, the aggregate commit floor in aFAULTEDSWEEPKeepsCOMMITTINGRatherThanSTALLING goes red, and the failure reads as a protocol defect in the sequencer rather than as the harness's own key collision, which is the misdiagnosis R8 was written to prevent.
